loc_455.loc_354: The increasing demand for resilient and sustainable food production necessitates a comprehensive understanding of rhizosphere microbial communities and their functional roles in enhancing plant health, nutrient acquisition, stress resilience, and crop productivity, thereby supporting food security and sustainable agriculture. However, soil microbiomes are composed of complex and unculturable communities of beneficial microorganisms that drive critical ecosystem functions, which traditional culture methods cannot capture. This limits the understanding of their roles and impacts on plant health and agricultural sustainability. Metagenomic tools have emerged as transformative approaches for characterizing microbial diversity in soil. Therefore, this review presents an overview of how metagenomic techniques can be harnessed to predict microbial community structures and their associated functional potentials, ultimately contributing to the development of resilient farming strategies. Next-generation sequencing and bioinformatics enable metagenomics to analyze microbial genetic material in soil and rhizospheres. This study provides insights into microbial diversity and profiles of key functional genes linked to nutrient availability and soil functions. We discuss the use of metagenomics tools to predict soil health and microbial functions for sustainable agroecosystems, emphasizing predictive models that help farmers optimize yields and minimize environmental impact. This review explores how metagenomics tools in agriculture can serve as a predictive model to transform our understanding of soil-microbe interactions. This advancement can facilitate the formulation of novel, more resilient, productive, and sustainable agricultural systems.

loc_462.loc_434: The soil and rhizosphere microbiomes are increasingly acknowledged as fundamental components for plant health, nutrient cycling, and resilient agriculture [1]. The rhizosphere is often referred to as the confined soil compartment intimately shaped by rhizodeposits and related microbes. It supports a multifaceted and beneficial consortium of microbes, comprising virus bacteria, archaea, and fungi [2]. These microbial populations engage in diverse interactions with plants, facilitating growth, augmenting stress tolerance, and nutrient mediation, which are vital for plant development [3]. Lidbury et al. [4] demonstrated that these beneficial rhizosphere microbiomes are capable of engaging in diverse functions, including solubilization of phosphate and transformation of atmospheric nitrogen (AN) into usable forms, as well as plant growth hormone synthesis. Similarly, they also help suppress harmful soil organisms by competing with and secreting antimicrobial substances [5].

loc_243.loc_225: Despite their critical importance, conventional microbiological methods such as culture-dependent techniques have encountered challenges in comprehensively characterizing the diversity and functions of soil and rhizosphere microbiomes [10]. Culturedependent techniques, which necessitate the in vitro proliferation of microorganisms, typically retrieve less than 2.5% of the entire community of microorganisms present in soil ecosystems [11]. Numerous soil microorganisms demonstrate resistance to cultivation, and those that are amenable to growth under laboratory conditions may not necessarily represent the most functionally pivotal constituents of the community of microbes [12]. This constraint has historically impeded efforts to elucidate the full spectrum of interactions among microorganisms and their ability to proliferate for the production and well-being of plants [13].

loc_243.loc_336: The advent of high-throughput sequencing techniques such as shotgun metagenomics has greatly transformed the investigation of soil and rhizosphere microbiomes. Metagenomic methodologies, such as shotgun sequencing, enable scientists to examine the entire gene pool of microbiome populations from environmental samples without cultivation, thereby eliminating the requirement for cultivation [14]. This approach has facilitated the characterization of previously uncharacterized microbiome taxa and the clarification of their functional diversities related to the cycling of nutrients, resistance to disease, and facilitation of plant development [15]. It has also helped in profiling the microbial metabolic pathways linked to plant growth and development, thus providing novel targets for microbiome engineering and sustainable agricultural practices [16].

loc_243.loc_446: Furthermore, Next-Generation Sequencing (NGS) has facilitated the advancement of predictive modeling and the strategic manipulation of microbiomes. By integrating metagenomic datasets with network analysis and machine learning models, scientists are able to identify critical microbial taxa as well as functions that underpin beneficial plant-microbe interactions [17]. This advancement has facilitated the development of bioinoculants and soil amendments, which are designed to recruit or augment beneficial microbial communities, thereby increasing crop productivity and resilience while diminishing the reliance on chemical inputs [18]. In extreme environments, such as arid agricultural systems, metagenomic investigations have revealed a high degree of microbial population and functional diversity [19].

loc_462.loc_122: In relation to Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) 2 (Zero Hunger), the application of metagenomics has significantly augmented food production by employing microbial technologies aimed at enhancing agricultural productivity, soil health, and the sustainability of farming practices. This approach facilitates the identification of beneficial microorganisms that can be utilized in the formulation of biofertilizers and biopesticides, thereby contributing to increased crop yields while concurrently reducing the dependence on harmful chemical agents [13]. In a similar vein, metagenomics constitutes a crucial component in the pursuit of SDG 13, specifically concerning climate change research, by facilitating comprehensive environmental monitoring. This capability allows for the comprehensive collection of data, which is instrumental in the development of adaptive strategies designed to mitigate the impacts of climate change and environmental monitoring and increase ecosystem resilience [20].

loc_462.loc_196: Therefore, this review explores the use of metagenomics to profile soil and rhizosphere microbial communities and their roles in sustainable agriculture. This study highlights modern techniques for predicting microbial composition, diversity, and functions, emphasizing their benefits for plant health, nutrient cycling, resistance to diseases, and stress tolerance. This review discusses the integration of metagenomic data with traditional farming and future research, including the use of machine learning, to improve sustainable agriculture and soil health.

loc_424.loc_439: 3 | Metagenomic Approaches for Revealing Microbiome Functions and Diversity

loc_243.loc_100: The field of microbial community research has experienced a transformative shift as a result of progress in NGS techniques. These innovations have empowered researchers to investigate the structure, diversity, and functional aspects of microbiomes with unprecedented precision. Two primary methodologies, amplicon sequencing (which uses markers such as 16S rRNA for studying bacteria as well as archaea and internal transcribed spacer (ITS) for fungal characterization) and shotgun metagenomics (Figures 1 and 2), constitute the foundational techniques utilized in the majority of microbiome investigations [70]. Complementing these methods is a swiftly advancing network of computational tools, functional profiling methods, and integrative multiomics strategies, which collectively extend the boundaries of microbiome science (Figure 3).

loc_240.loc_138: 3.1 | Shotgun Sequencing Techniques and Amplicon Sequencing (16S/ITS): Comparison of Their Strengths and Limitations

loc_462.loc_86: Amplicon sequencing (Figure 1), which focuses on the 16S rRNA gene (which serves as a critical molecular marker for the characterization and identification of bacterial and archaeal communities) and the ITS region, which serves as a critical molecular marker for fungal communities, has been a fundamental technique in microbial soil ecology [71]. This approach involves amplification via polymerase chain reaction (PCR) of conserved genetic markers, followed by sequencing and subsequent taxonomic classification. Its advantages include its cost-effectiveness, scalability, and capacity to generate reliable genus-level and occasionally species-level taxonomic profiles across extensive sample collections, especially in resource-constrained environments [72].

loc_462.loc_174: Amplicon sequencing, despite its effectiveness, has significant limitations. The limitation of this method is associated primarily with the selection of primers and the subsequent amplification process in polymerase chain reaction (PCR), which may alter the representation of particular taxa [73]. Its taxonomic resolution capability is predominantly constrained to the genus level, rendering species-level identification frequently unreliable, particularly for phylogenetically proximate organisms [72]. Furthermore, amplicon sequencing provides only indirect inferences about functional potential, as it does not capture the full complement of gene representation within the community [74].

loc_243.loc_430: In contrast to targeted approaches involving amplicon sequencing, shotgun metagenomics (Figure 2) involves sequencing all DNA present within a given sample, thereby encompassing not only bacterial and archaeal DNA but also that of viruses, fungi, and other eukaryotic organisms [13]. This methodology facilitates extensive taxonomic profiling with significantly higher resolution, often extending to the species or even strain level, and facilitates the direct evaluation of functional genes and metabolic pathways. Shotgun metagenomics is particularly efficient in identifying rare or low-abundance taxa and in characterizing the functional diversities of microbial communities [75]. Nonetheless, the limitations associated with shotgun metagenomics include its increased financial cost, increased computational requirements, and the need for deeper sequencing efforts to obtain adequate coverage, particularly in complex or low-biomass samples [76]. The data analysis process is more intricate, necessitating robust bioinformatics pipelines and considerable computational resources [77].

loc_462.loc_372: Comparative analyses have demonstrated that although both methods can yield similar genus-level profiles for bacterial, archaeal and fungal communities, shotgun metagenomics consistently outperforms amplicon sequencing in achieving higher species-level resolution, identifying rare taxa, and predicting functional genes [78]. Nevertheless, for fungal studies, the concordance between shotgun metagenomics and ITS amplicon sequencing is frequently limited, underscoring the necessity for methodological selection tailored to specific research objectives and target organisms [79].

loc_243.loc_409: Figure 1 above illustrates the workflow of amplicon sequencing, which constitutes a robust and standardized framework for characterizing microbial communities, systematically integrating wet-laboratory sample preparation with advanced downstream bioinformatic analysis [82]. Beginning with DNA extraction and marker-gene PCR amplification followed by high-throughput sequencing, the pipeline facilitates highly targeted data acquisition. The bioinformatic core incorporates stringent quality control, deionizing, and sequence clustering procedures (employing tools such as FastQC, DADA2, and VSEARCH) to minimize PCR-derived artifacts and sequencing errors, thereby enabling the generation of reliable amplicon sequence variants (ASVs) or operational taxonomic units (OTUs). In parallel, taxonomic assignment against curated reference databases (e.g., SILVA, Greengenes) and functional inference via Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG)-based annotation support a comprehensive, dual-perspective analysis that resolves both community composition ("who is present") and putative metabolic potential ("what functional capacities are encoded"). The subsequent integration of these complementary abundance matrices into ecological diversity indices and statistical visualization workflows provides a rigorous and reproducible framework for extracting biologically meaningful insights from complex metagenomic datasets.

loc_462.loc_284: Figure 2 schematically depicts a shotgun metagenomics workflow that employs an assembly-first strategy to characterize the taxonomic composition, functional repertoire, and antibiotic resistance determinants of microbial communities [83]. Following initial quality control to obtain high-fidelity sequencing reads, de novo assembly and subsequent gene prediction are performed to generate a nonredundant catalog of unigenes. This centralized gene catalog is subsequently analyzed via three parallel annotation pipelines: one for taxonomic assignment via the Micro NR database; another for metabolic and phenotypic profiling on the basis of core functional resources (using KEGG, CAZy, eggNOG, VFDB, and PHI); and a third for resistome analysis focused on antibiotic resistance genes and mobile genetic elements (CARDs and MGEs).

loc_462.loc_395: Downstream statistical analyses integrate these multilayered annotations to elucidate community ecological dynamics. In particular, species- and function-level matrices are subjected to multivariate ordination and diversity analyses (NMDS, PCoA, PCA, and alpha diversity metrics) in conjunction with nonparametric and machine learning-based differential abundance testing (LEfSe, random forest [RF], MetaGenomeSeq, Anosim, iPATH) to identify discriminant biomarkers among experimental groups. In parallel, the resistome-specific branch yields a focused characterization of antibiotic resistance, delineating the diversity, differential abundance, and putative host-species associations of resistance determinants, thereby providing a comprehensive assessment of community functional potential and biosafety risks.

loc_460.loc_432: 3.1.1 | Factors Influencing the Choice Between Amplicon and Shotgun Sequencing in Soil and Rhizosphere Metagenomic Studies

loc_243.loc_56: Soil and rhizosphere samples present specific methodological challenges for metagenomic analyses that directly influence sequencing strategies. Amplicon sequencing of taxonomic marker genes (e.g., 16S rRNA, ITS) is often preferred for soil community surveys because it is sensitive for detecting microbial taxa in complex microbial assemblages, is cost-effective for large sample sets, and benefits from comprehensive 16S reference databases covering diverse soil microbial communities [84].

loc_243.loc_115: In contrast, shotgun metagenomic sequencing not only detects microbial taxa but also offers higher functional resolution for soil microbiomes (e.g., nutrient cycling genes and plant growth-promoting traits). However, it requires high-quality microbial DNA and is hindered by high organic matter and humic substances, which interfere with DNA extraction and sequencing [85].

loc_243.loc_211: However, choosing between amplicon-based methods and shotgun metagenomic sequencing for soil microbiome studies depends on soil traits and study design. Amplicon sequencing (e.g., 16S rRNA, and ITS) is preferred when the focus is on taxonomic profiling of highly diverse soil communities with hundreds of taxa per gram; when many samples must be processed on a limited budget (e.g., greenhouse trials with many replicates); when detecting low-abundance taxa is important, targeted PCR improves sensitivity; and when comprehensive, well-curated marker gene databases (e.g., SILVA and Greengenes) with good coverage of soil bacteria are available [86].

loc_243.loc_314: However, amplicon sequencing has important limitations for soil microbial communities, including PCR bias from primer mismatches with uncharacterized taxa and an inability to directly infer functional potential (e.g., genes for nutrient cycling or plant growth promotion) [87]. Thus, shotgun metagenomic sequencing is preferred when (1) functional annotation is the main goal, such as detecting and characterizing genes for phosphate solubilization, indole-3-acetic acid (IAA) biosynthesis, or nitrogen fixation in biofertilizer development; (2) strain-level resolution is needed to distinguish closely related rhizosphere isolates; and (3) high-quality metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs) are needed for genome-resolved and comparative analyses [88].

loc_243.loc_402: The main drawbacks of shotgun metagenomics include high organic matter and humic substances that inhibit library preparation and sequencing and abundant host DNA in rhizosphere samples, which reduces microbial sequencing depth and often requires host DNA depletion or microbial DNA enrichment [89]. loc_192.loc_431: 3.2 | Computational Tools and Pipelines for Metagenomics Analysis

loc_243.loc_468: The explosion of microbiome data has spurred the advancement of a wide spectrum of computational tools and analytical pipelines, each specifically designed to address distinct sequencing techniques and research investigations.

QIIME2 accommodates both ASV workflows and OTU workflows, and it provides plugins for denoising, including DADA2 and Deblur, as well as integration with multiple databases of reference sequences such as SILVA and Greengenes [90]. Similarly, Mothur is a well-established pipeline specifically designed for the processing of 16S rRNA gene sequences, offering capabilities for robust clustering, chimera detection, and taxonomic profiling [91]. DADA2, a high-resolution denoising algorithm, enhances the sensitivity and specificity of amplicon data by inferring exact sequence variants [92].

loc_462.loc_299: However, in shotgun metagenomics sequencing, several pivotal computations (pipelines) are utilized for the analysis of metagenomic data (Figure 2). Among these, MG-RAST serves as an automated platform for facilitating both taxonomic and functional annotations through the employment of diverse reference databases [93]. Likewise, MEGAN offers a robust framework for the interactive exploration and scrutiny of extensive metagenomic datasets, enabling both taxonomic and functional classification while seamlessly integrating with high-throughput aligners such as DIAMOND [94]. In the same vein, Kraken2 is recognized for its exceptional speed as a k-mer-based classifier, delivering high-accuracy taxonomic assignments for both amplicon and shotgun sequence data [95]. Moreover, HUMAnN3 is proficient at functional profiling, reconstructing metabolic pathways from metagenomic or metatranscriptomic data by mapping sequence reads to gene families and pathways through databases such as KEGG, UniRef, and MetaCyc [96, 97]. Similarly, PICRUSt2 is tailored for predictive functional profiling via 16S rRNA gene data, inferring the potential functionality of microbial communities by correlating taxa with known gene content from reference genomes [74].

loc_454.loc_417: 3.3 | Predictive Functional Profiling: Transitioning From Taxonomic Classification to Functional Assessment

loc_462.loc_468: The primary objective of microbiome research is to move beyond basic taxonomic composition and elucidate the functional capabilities of microbial communities (Table 1). Predictive functional profiling efforts seek to bridge this gap by leveraging taxonomic data to decipher the incidence of genes and metabolic pathways.

These predictions are instrumental in formulating hypotheses concerning microbial community function, particularly when shotgun metagenomics is not feasible. However, the precision of these predictions is constrained by the quality of taxonomic assignments, the completeness of reference databases, and the presumption that phylogenetically similar taxa possess analogous functional repertoires. In agriculture, 16S rRNA gene sequencing elucidates the compositional structure of microbial diversity but is not sensitive enough to identify crucial functional potential or ecologically relevant microbiome impacts that affect soil fertility and crop growth, necessitating careful interpretation [99].

loc_243.loc_240: Conversely, shotgun metagenomics, a technique that involves sequencing the whole complement of genes directly within a community, affords a more dependable and exhaustive perspective of functional potential (Figure 2) [75]. Sequencing reads can be aligned to gene databases and metabolic pathways via the COG, eggNOG, and KEGG databases, facilitating the detailed characterization of the community of microorganisms and their metabolism and functional diversity [100]. This approach is efficient when integrated with pathway-centric tools such as HUMAnN3, which enables profiling of the abundance and completeness of metabolic pathways across samples [1, 101].

By further extending this analysis to the protein level, metaproteomics facilitates characterization of the expressed proteome within a microbial community by identifying and quantifying microbial proteins [105]. Concurrently, metabolomics analyzes the metabolites (intermediate products) synthesized or produced by microbiota, thereby offering a holistic perspective of the biochemical products and ecological impacts of microbiomes in the soil [107]. loc_416.loc_262: 4 | Applications of Metagenomic Tools in Sustainable Agriculture

loc_462.loc_350: Metagenomic tools have emerged as pivotal and cutting-edge tools in the advancement of agricultural sustainability, providing an unparalleled understanding of the diversity, functionality, structure, and makeup of soil and plant-associated microbial communities. These tools have facilitated the direct sequencing and analysis of genetic materials obtained from environmental samples, thereby circumventing the limitations inherent in traditional culture-based techniques. This approach reveals the extensive array of microorganisms that are integral to soil health, plant growth, and ecosystem resilience [13].

loc_462.loc_409: Metagenomics presents a robust scientific method for achieving SDG 2 by 2030 by facilitating innovative solutions for food security and sustainable agriculture. This involves developing crops that are resilient to climate change, increasing drought and salinity tolerance, and directly supporting SDG2's goals of eradicating hunger and promoting sustainable agriculture to ensure food availability for everyone [145].

loc_243.loc_137: The utilization of metagenomics tools, including QIIME2, MGRAST, and Kraken2, in sustainable agriculture has significantly enhanced the monitoring of soil health. As a dynamic ecosystem, soil harbors an intricate community of beneficial microorganisms that facilitate nutrient cycling, decomposition of organic matter, and contaminant degradation (Table 1) [11]. Metagenomics provides a comprehensive framework for characterizing these microbial communities by identifying both the taxonomic constituents and functional genes within the soil matrix, particularly the rhizosphere of the soil (Table 1) [146]. Similarly, through the monitoring of microbial indicator processes related to soil fertility, such as those involved in fixing AN, solubilizing phosphate, and decomposing organic matter, researchers and farmers can evaluate the biological quality of soils with unprecedented precision [147]. This approach has also revolutionized the detection of alterations in the community of microorganisms resulting from land management practices, environmental pollution, or climatic changes, thereby offering early indicators of soil degradation or contamination. Robust microbial indicators through metagenomic approaches are now critical for sustainable land management and conservation strategies, as they ensure the sustainable maintenance of soil quality and productivity [148].

loc_243.loc_277: Similarly, metagenomics tools in agriculture have fundamentally transformed the formulation of biofertilizers, which are microbial preparations used to augment and ameliorate crop development and soil nutrient status. Through the analysis of genetic material from soil and rhizosphere ecosystems, metagenomics facilitates the identification of beneficial microorganisms with traits related to nutrient mineralization and fixation and the production of phytohormones favorable for plant growth, thereby decreasing the dependence on chemical fertilizers and mitigating environmental consequences [13, 149]. Additionally, metagenomics supports the discovery of genes associated with these beneficial traits (Table 1), advancing bioengineering and synthetic biology strategies to engineer next-generation biofertilizers with improved efficacy and customized functionalities [32]. The integration of metagenomics with high-throughput screening and other omics technologies is promoting the advancement of sustainable, environmentally favorable solutions to address the growing global food demand [146].

loc_243.loc_424: Furthermore, metagenomic tools such as CARD (antibiotic resistance gene database), MetaGeneMark and HUMAnN offer robust potential in biological control and disease suppression for the detection of antagonistic microorganisms and functional genes involved in pathogen suppression [150, 151]. Soil-borne pathogens and pests present major risks to crop production. However, metagenomics enables the characterization of microbial gene clusters and taxa linked to natural disease resistance, such as those encoding antibiotics, lytic enzymes, and siderophores [147]. Elucidating the mechanisms by which beneficial microorganisms inhibit pathogen proliferation enables researchers to devise effective biocontrol agents and disease-suppressive soil amendments, thereby reducing the dependence on synthetic agrochemicals and promoting agroecosystem sustainability [28]. Furthermore, functional metagenomics, coupled with network analysis, bolsters the targeted recruitment or augmentation of beneficial microbes within the rhizosphere, thereby enhancing plant protection and contributing to overall ecosystem health (Table 1) [152].

loc_462.loc_56: However, the application of metagenomic tools in climate-smart agriculture is gaining significant attention, particularly because of the pivotal roles played by soil microbes in processes such as carbon sequestration, mitigation of greenhouse gas emissions, and bolstering crop tolerance against stressors such as salinity and drought. Shotgun metagenomics analysis of maize roots cultivated under long-term fertilization regimes revealed that although the overall abundance of microbial functional genes was comparable, the diversity and specific metabolic pathways exhibited marked variation across different treatments [39, 40]. Notably, organic fertilization was associated with an increased abundance of beneficial functional diversity related to nutrient cycling and plant growth promotion, indicating that biofertilizers enhance soil health and sustainability more effectively than chemical fertilizers do. Additional studies have shown that the excessive use of agrochemicals (synthetic fertilizers) can disrupt the structure of microbial communities, decrease beneficial interactions, and lead to increased soil acidification. loc_234.loc_358: 7 | Challenges and Future Directions for Metagenomics as a Predictive Tool in Agricultural Sustainability

loc_243.loc_416: Metagenomics has fundamentally transformed the investigation of soil microbiomes, providing unparalleled insights into microbial diversity and function, which are critical for the maintenance of sustainable agricultural production. Nevertheless, the use of metagenomics as a tool for predicting agricultural sustainability at the field scale presents several substantial challenges and opportunities for advancement.

loc_243.loc_468: Technical constraints, such as sequencing depth, database selection or biases, and the reproducibility of outcomes, continue to represent a significant impediment, particularly within intricate and variable soil environments. These limitations can adversely affect the precision and dependability of metagenomic predictions [170].

These challenges obstruct thorough functional annotation, resulting in many microbial taxa whose metabolic roles remain unclear [9, 170]. Many existing tools and reference databases have been optimized for human-associated samples, which results in diminished performance and interpretability within agricultural contexts [171]. Furthermore, the extensive data generated necessitate robust computational resources and standardized workflows to ensure consistent and comparable results across studies [31].

loc_462.loc_247: A significant future direction involves the incorporation of multiomics techniques that merge metagenomics with meta-transcriptomics, metabolomics, proteomics and soil physicochemical data, which is important for comprehensively understanding the microbial community and its functional characterization [102, 103]. Similarly, a meticulously curated database, such as RefSoil, is needed to enhance the evaluation of soil microbiomes [171]. These comprehensive strategies can effectively link microbial community structure to ecosystem processes and agricultural sustainability, thereby offering a more thorough understanding of soil health and resilience [172]. However, harmonizing these diverse datasets presents analytical and technical challenges, requires interdisciplinary collaboration and advanced statistical methodologies [102, 103], and translating laboratory predictions to real-world and field-scale applications represents another essential challenge.

loc_462.loc_292: Many research findings remain confined to controlled experimental settings. Translation insights into practical, scalable agricultural practices mandate field validation, the establishment of standardized protocols, and the development of accessible decision-support tools for farmers [11].

loc_462.loc_350: However, the integration of machine learning annotation, single-cell genomics, AI and long-read sequencing holds significant promise for precision agriculture, facilitating the analysis of complex, multisource data to generate practicable insights. loc_462.loc_468: Metagenomic tools have advanced from cataloging microbial diversity to offering predictive insights for sustainable agriculture. loc_243.loc_56: Metagenomics, employed as a predictive tool, provides significant insights into soil health and microbial diversity, thereby facilitating sustainable agricultural practices that contribute directly to the realization of SDGs 2 (Zero Hunger) and 13 (Climate Action).

loc_243.loc_137: Combining metagenomics with remote sensing, IoT sensors, and machine learning further enhances precision agriculture through real-time monitoring for adaptive management of soil health and crop performance [172]. These advancements promise improved food security and soil health by reducing chemical inputs, increasing yields, and fostering resilient agroecosystems [11]. The shift from descriptive metagenomics to predictive metagenomics is crucial for sustainable, microbiome-informed agriculture, meeting food demand while protecting the environment.
